reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Subacute, often asymmetric and multifocal sensory loss that is non-length-dependent, affecting the face, trunk and proximal limbs as well as the distal extremities.
Prominent sensory ataxia and pseudoathetosis with preserved muscle strength reflect selective large-fibre dorsal root ganglion loss.
Early painful paraesthesiae and loss of all sensory modalities, with areflexia, are characteristic.
Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) with small-cell lung carcinoma is the commonest association; it may occur in isolation or as part of paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis.
Nerve conduction studies show reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials with normal or near-normal motor conduction.
The neuronopathy frequently precedes the cancer diagnosis, so a thorough malignancy search is essential.
Response to immunotherapy is usually poor, and tumour treatment offers the best chance of stabilisation.
Key mimics to exclude are Sjogren-related ganglionopathy, platinum chemotherapy toxicity and pyridoxine excess.
reference.pathophysiology: An immune response against intracellular onconeural antigens (most often HuD, expressed by small-cell lung carcinoma) targets the sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia. Cytotoxic T-cell mediated inflammation and neuronal destruction within the ganglia produce a ganglionopathy affecting both large and small fibres. Because the primary sensory cell body is destroyed, deficits are non-length-dependent and largely irreversible, and secondary degeneration of the central posterior columns and peripheral sensory axons follows.
additionalDifferentials: vitamin B12 or vitamin E deficiency
additionalInvestigations: serum and CSF anti-Hu (ANNA-1) and paraneoplastic antibody panel
nerve conduction studies and EMG demonstrating a sensory ganglionopathy pattern
anti-Ro/La antibodies and Schirmer test to assess for Sjogren syndrome
whole-body FDG-PET/CT and CT chest for occult malignancy
MRI spine looking for posterior column T2 hyperintensity
vitamin B12 and vitamin B6 levels
CSF analysis for pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands
redFlags: rapid progression to disabling sensory ataxia and loss of ambulation
associated autonomic failure or gastrointestinal dysmotility
constitutional features (weight loss, night sweats) suggesting malignancy
bulbar or respiratory signs indicating overlap with encephalomyelitis
reference.prognosis: Recovery of sensory function is usually poor because the ganglion neurons are destroyed; the realistic therapeutic goal is stabilisation through treatment of the underlying tumour. Functional outcome is often limited by persistent sensory ataxia.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the deficit as a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy and missing the non-length-dependent pattern.
Failing to screen for Sjogren syndrome, the principal non-paraneoplastic cause.
Not pursuing small-cell lung carcinoma when anti-Hu antibodies are positive.
Overlooking a drug or vitamin cause such as platinum agents or pyridoxine excess.
references: Camdessanche JP, et al. The pattern and diagnostic criteria of sensory neuronopathy. Brain.
Graus F, Delattre JY, et al. Recommended diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes.
